lessonLine: Grade 11 · Algebra II · Topic 9: Conic Sections · Lesson 9-2 — Circles
objectives: Derive the equation of a circle given its center and radius.
Complete the square to find the center and radius of a circle.
Determine the relative positions of a circle and a line in the plane.
Solve a system of equations with one linear equation and one equation of a circle algebraically and verify the solution by graphing.

outcome: Students will derive the equation of a circle from its center and radius using the distance formula (objective 1; HSG.GPE.A.1).
Students will complete the square to find the center and the radius of a circle given by an equation (objective 2; HSA.SSE.B.3).
Students will determine whether a line misses, touches or cuts a circle (objective 3).
Students will solve a line-circle system algebraically and verify the solution by graphing (objective 4; HSA.REI.C.7).
Three teaching days this week. If time runs short, cut Smart Production — never the Mastery Gate.
preclass: Pre-session home journey (already issued, four slides): watch “How To Find The Center and Radius of a Circle”, study one worked example for $x^{2}+y^{2}-6x+4y-12=0$, answer four ungraded readiness questions. Submitted on the LMS before class.

Readiness questions: the center and radius of $(x+1)^{2}+(y-4)^{2}=49$; the center and radius of $x^{2}+y^{2}+8x-2y+8=0$; the equation with center $(2,-3)$ and radius $4$; the equation with center the origin through $(3,4)$.
Evidence: the LMS answers feed the Diagnose.
diagTool: 3-question Quizizz (≤ 4 minutes) — the slide-4 checks: complete the square for $x^{2}+6x$; find the distance from $(0,0)$ to $(3,4)$; solve $x^{2}-2x-8=0$.
diagGap: Expected gaps — Q1: the $-9$ is left out. Q3: the roots are given with the wrong signs.
Routing: 0–1 correct → re-teach completing the square and factoring.  2 → straight to the circle equation.  3 → begin Investigate early.
instruction: Slide 5 — The equation of a circle (objective 1; HSG.GPE.A.1). $(x-h)^{2}+(y-k)^{2}=r^{2}$ comes from the distance formula; center $(3,-2)$, $r=5$ gives $(x-3)^{2}+(y+2)^{2}=25$; center $(-4,1)$ through $(-1,5)$ has $r^{2}=25$.

Slide 6 — Completing the square (objective 2; HSA.SSE.B.3). $x^{2}+y^{2}-6x+4y-12=0$ becomes $(x-3)^{2}+(y+2)^{2}=25$; $x^{2}+y^{2}+8x-2y+8=0$ has center $(-4,1)$, $r=3$; $2x^{2}+2y^{2}-12x+8y-8=0$ has $r=\sqrt{17}$.
Slide 7 — A line and a circle (objective 3). With $x^{2}+y^{2}=25$: $y=3$ cuts at $(\pm4,3)$; $y=5$ touches at $(0,5)$; $y=-7$ misses. Compare the distance $d$ from the center with $r$.

Slide 8 — Solving the system (objective 4; HSA.REI.C.7). $x^{2}+y^{2}=25$ with $y=x+1$ gives $(3,4)$ and $(-4,-3)$; $(x-2)^{2}+(y+1)^{2}=8$ with $y=x-3$ gives $(0,-3)$ and $(4,1)$; $y=3x+10$ is tangent to $x^{2}+y^{2}=10$ at $(-3,1)$.
Narration focus — the number on the right is $r^{2}$; flip the signs for the center; a repeated root means a tangent.
quickCheck: On whiteboards, 60 seconds: the circle $(x+1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}=36$ — write the center and the radius.
Expected: center $(-1,2)$, radius $6$. Watch for $(1,-2)$ and for radius $36$.
guided: Two identical “Give it a go” problems, worked with the teacher:
(1) Find the center and radius of $x^{2}+y^{2}-10x+6y+18=0$.  (2) Write the equation with center $(0,3)$ and radius $\sqrt{7}$.
Worked live; students self-mark and circle their OWN first error.
independent: “Choose Your Route” sheet with live Pear Deck feedback. Routes name the task, not the student.

PRACTICE — Secure the method. Six cards: read the center and radius, write the equation, complete the square; then find the error and sketch one circle on the grid. Done when: the center is read with the signs flipped and the right-hand side is treated as $r^{2}$.
APPLY — Use it in context. A plaza and a path, a radio tower, a lake and a path. Done when: the center is placed first and each answer says what it means.

INVESTIGATE — Find out why. Derive the equation, show a tangent by a repeated root, and prove the tangency condition $c^{2}=r^{2}(1+m^{2})$. Done when: the argument starts from the distance formula or a repeated solution.
Page 3: compare three routes, judge three claims, test a What if...? idea. Every student sits the same Mastery Gate.
production: Non-routine transfer task — this context has not appeared in practice (slide 11).
A model circular reflecting pool in the Hira Cultural District has the equation $x^{2}+y^{2}-8x-6y=0$ (metres). The model values are invented for practice.

(a) Find the center and radius and show the pool passes through the origin. (b) A walkway along $y=x$ crosses the pool: find where it enters and leaves, and the length over water. (c) A walkway along $y=8$: does it miss, touch or cut the pool?
Answers: (a) $(x-4)^{2}+(y-3)^{2}=25$, center $(4,3)$, $r=5$. (b) $(0,0)$ and $(7,7)$, length $7\sqrt{2}\approx9.9$ m. (c) distance from the center $=5=r$, so it touches at $(4,8)$.
Students then hand their reasoning to the AI challenger.
criteria: Minimum standard: standard form, center and radius, both intersection points, units (m).
Role of AI: challenger only — “Challenge my reasoning and point out any step I have not justified.” Never “solve this”.
Completed independently: the written justification for (a)–(c).
evidence: “Time to Check” — one individual task. No notes, no partner, no AI.
1. Write the equation with center $(-3,2)$ and radius $4$.  2. Center and radius of $x^{2}+y^{2}+6x-4y-12=0$.  3. Solve $x^{2}+y^{2}=20$ with $y=x+2$.
Done when: question 2 shows the completing-the-square line and question 3 gives both points.
Scored live in Pear Deck and logged in the Impact Dashboard.
refinement: Students revise their pool reasoning using the AI challenger’s feedback and the teacher’s micro-conference note.

Final product (Canva one-pager, photographed solution, or 45-second voice note): the equation in standard form, the walkway intersections, ONE non-example (radius read as $r^{2}$), and why a repeated root means a tangent.
differentiation: PRACTICE — Secure the method. Six cards, a find-the-error line and a sketch. Done when: the center is read with the signs flipped.
APPLY — Use it in context. A plaza, a tower, a lake and a path. Done when: the center is placed first.
INVESTIGATE — Find out why. A derivation, a tangent and the tangency condition. Done when: the argument starts from the distance formula.
No student is labelled; every student sits the same Mastery Gate.
saudi: Hira Cultural District plaza and pool, a radio tower and a lake; invented values.
exams: SAT — Geometry and Trigonometry: $x^{2}+y^{2}-6x+8y=c$ is a circle of radius $7$, so $c=24$. Trap: using $c=49$.
GAT (Qudurat) — the radius of $x^{2}+y^{2}-4x+6y-3=0$ versus $3$: $r=4$, so the radius is greater. Trap: taking $r^{2}=16$ as the radius.
SAAT (Tahsili) — the line $y=x+k$ with $k>0$ is tangent to $x^{2}+y^{2}=8$ when $k=4$. Trap: $k=\sqrt{8}$.
adaptive: Entry branch — the Quizizz result routes each student to the re-teach table, straight to the new content, or the Investigate prompt.
Mid-lesson branch — Pear Deck flags error patterns during independent practice; flagged students get a 2-minute micro-conference while others continue.
Exit branch — the Mastery Gate routes each student: PASS → Enrichment & Challenge; NOT YET → Targeted Learning Clinic at the start of the next lesson.
Routing is communicated privately through the LMS, never read aloud.
publication: Published to the class LMS portfolio; the strongest go on the Mathematics Department wall.

plan2026.tools: Quizizz (diagnostic) · Pear Deck (live practice feedback) · Whiteboards · Graphing technology · Canva (final product) · Squared paper
plan2026.resources: Lesson presentation (15 slides) · “Choose Your Route” activity (3 pages) · Wayground kick-off
competencies: Writing the equation of a circle and reading its center and radius, including after completing the square.
Solving a line-circle system and verifying it on a graph.
technology: Quizizz live diagnostic with instant gap analysis.
Graphing technology to check the intersection points of a line and a circle.
reallife: A plaza, a pool and a walkway: where does the path cross the water?
A radio tower: who is inside the covered area?
values: Accuracy — every sign is written down before it is used.
Precision — exact answers first, decimals only at the end.
soft: Explaining in words why the right-hand side is $r^{2}$.
hard: Using a repeated root to show a tangent.
phases: FIKR Phase 1 — Diagnose. 3-question Quizizz: completing the square, distance, solving a quadratic. Results read as a gap map and used to route students.
FIKR Phase 2 — Targeted Instruction. The equation of a circle; completing the square; a line and a circle; solving the system.
FIKR Phase 3 — Practice. Two identical “Give it a go” problems; then students choose a route and may switch. Compare routes and judge the claim. Pear Deck feedback.
FIKR Phase 4 — Production. Hira Cultural District reflecting pool; AI as challenger only.
FIKR Phase 5 — Proof of Learning. “Time to Check”. No notes, no partner, no AI.
FIKR Phase 6 — Smart Production. Design a circle and a line, find their intersections, swap and test; publish to the LMS portfolio.
assessment: Diagnostic quiz — gap map, not a grade.
Whiteboard check (80% threshold) and “Give it a go” — self-marked.
Project task sheet against its “Done when…” criteria.
“Time to Check” — Mastery Gate, scored live.
Final product graded on reasoning and clarity.
plan2026.closure: Two minutes of peer show-and-tell, then: “Which is harder — reading the signs in the equation, or deciding whether the line touches the circle?”
plan2026.homework: Upload the final product to the LMS portfolio. Pear Deck practice set (12 questions, choose your route). Schoology homework quiz for Lesson 9-2. Watch the flipped video for the next lesson. Clinic group: bring your Time to Check paper.

classwork.subtitle: Show all your working. Read the vertex with the signs flipped, divide 4p by 4, and measure to the focus and the directrix. A correct answer with no working is only half an answer.

sections.h: Part A — Focus, directrix and the equation
text: 1.  A parabola has focus $(0,2)$ and directrix $y=-2$. For the point $P(4,2)$, find $PF$ and $PD$. Is $P$ on the parabola? Then derive the equation using $PF=PD$.
2.  Derive the equation of the parabola with focus $(0,5)$ and directrix $y=-5$. State $p$.
3.  Write the equation of the parabola with focus $(0,-4)$ and directrix $y=4$. Which way does it open?

sections.h: Part B — Reading the equation and the graph
text: 4.  Find the vertex, $p$, the focus, the directrix and the axis of symmetry.
5.  Find the vertex, $p$, the focus and the directrix. Which way does it open?
6.  The graph shows a parabola. Its vertex and focus are marked. Read them, then write the equation in standard form and the directrix.

sections.h: Part C — Graphing from key features
text: 7.  Graph $(x-1)^{2}=8\,(y+1)$ on the grid. Mark the vertex, the focus and the directrix, and the two points at the height of the focus.
8.  Graph $y^{2}=-8x$ on the grid. Mark the vertex, the focus and the directrix, and the two points at the height of the focus.
9.  Complete the square and find the vertex, the focus and the directrix.
10.  Complete the square and find the vertex, the focus and the directrix.
11.  Divide first, then complete the square. Find the vertex, the focus and the directrix.

sections.h: Part E — In context and in your own words
text: 12.  A model fountain jet on the Jeddah waterfront has its apex at $(0,8)$ and lands at $(\pm12,\,0)$ (metres, model values). Write its equation and find the focus. How high is the jet at $x=6$?
13.  A model satellite dish is $1.8$ m wide and $0.27$ m deep. Put the vertex at the origin, find $4p$ and say how far the receiver sits from the vertex.
14.  Show that the width of $x^{2}=4py$ at the height of the focus is $4\lvert p\rvert$. Use it to find the two points of $x^{2}=20y$ at that height.

pbl.title: Jeddah Satellite Dish Installer
pbl.subtitle: A 20-minute group project. Work in fours. Every member signs the sheet.
pbl.driving: A Jeddah installer has four dishes and one receiver arm that is 1.1 m long. Which dishes can hold the receiver exactly at the focus, and what does the shape of the dish tell you?
situation: A classroom model (invented for practice, not real figures): each dish is a parabola with its vertex at the origin, opening upward. Its width and depth are in the table. The receiver must sit at the focus, a distance $p$ above the vertex.

For each dish the group finds $4p$ from the rim point, writes the equation, finds $p$, and says whether a $1.1$ m arm is long enough. Then the group explains how the depth of a dish changes its focal length.
steps: For each dish, write the rim point $(x_{1},y_{1})$: half the width across, the full depth up. Write $x^{2}=4py$ with the rim point substituted.
Find $4p$ and $p$ for every dish and write each equation. Fill the table.
Which dishes can hold the receiver at the focus with a $1.1$ m arm? Check one dish: the rim point is equally far from the focus and the directrix.
What happens to $p$ as the dishes get deeper for their width? Which dish is the most tightly curved?
One sentence for the installer: how can you tell where the receiver goes from the width and depth alone?

standards: Choose and produce an equivalent form of an expression to reveal and explain properties of the quantity represented by the expression.
Solve a simple system consisting of a linear equation and a quadratic equation in two variables algebraically and graphically.
Derive the equation of a circle of given center and radius using the Pythagorean Theorem; complete the square to find the center and radius of a circle given by an equation.
